title: Genesis
summary: The foundational book of beginnings, tracing creation, human rebellion, the flood, Babel, and the patriarchal promises.
historical_context: Genesis gathers the Bible's opening stories and ancestral traditions into a theological account of how God's purposes for the world and for Israel begin.
ancient_near_east_context: Its creation, flood, and covenant narratives engage common ancient Near Eastern themes while recasting them around the one sovereign Creator and covenant Lord.
literary_context: Genesis opens the Pentateuch and moves from cosmic beginnings to family saga, linking primeval history with the story of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph.
covenantal_significance: Genesis introduces the promises of seed, land, and blessing that shape the rest of Scripture and point toward the nations' blessing.

interpretive_notes.note: Read Genesis as theological foundation for the whole canon rather than as a detached preface.
Keep the primeval chapters and the patriarchal narratives together; they work as one unfolding promise story.

common_questions: How do creation and covenant fit together in Genesis?
What is the significance of Abraham in Genesis?
authorship_positions: Many scholars see a composite work shaped over time
date_ranges: Critical: final shaping often placed in the exilic or post-exilic period
original_audience: Israel formed by covenant and delivered into the land promise
historical_setting: The Exodus, wilderness, and land-promise setting of the Torah
interpretive_disputes: How to read narrative and law together

scripture_references.notes: the fall and exile from Eden
the call and promise to Abram

related_objects.notes: the call that launches the promise line

hebraic_worldview: Creation is ordered sacred space, and the family line of promise carries blessing, memory, and land.
second_temple_context: Second Temple readers treated Genesis as the foundational story of creation, Abrahamic promise, and hope for restoration.
canonical_context: Genesis begins the canon with creation, fall, promise, and election so later books can read Israel's story within blessing and restoration.
later_christian_reception: Christians have long read Genesis as the opening frame for creation, sin, covenant, and promise fulfilled in Christ.
